passages.title: Chapter 0: Before creation
passages.text: Before creation: Stillness, and a single word of command. When: Before time.

passages.title: Chapter 1: The beginning
passages.text: The beginning: A hot, dense beginning, and space itself stretching. When: The first instant, about 13.8 billion years ago.

passages.title: Chapter 2: The first light
passages.text: The first light: From glowing plasma to the oldest light we can see. When: About 380,000 years after the beginning.

passages.title: Chapter 3: The dark ages and first stars
passages.text: The dark ages and the first stars: Out of darkness, a web of unseen matter and the first starlight. When: About 100 to 200 million years after the beginning.

passages.title: Chapter 4: A vast heaven
passages.text: A vast heaven: Space itself grows, and the light crossing it stretches. When: From about 1 billion years after the beginning.

passages.title: Chapter 5: Seven heavens and the galaxies
passages.text: Seven heavens and the galaxies: From our own galaxy to the edge of what we can see. When: From about 3 billion years after the beginning.

passages.title: Chapter 6: Stars and iron
passages.text: Stars and iron: How stars forge the elements, and scatter them. When: About 6 billion years after the beginning.

passages.title: Chapter 7: The Sun and its course
passages.text: The Sun and its course: A star is born, and each body keeps its orbit. When: 4.567 billion years ago.

passages.title: Chapter 8: The earth spread out
passages.text: The earth spread out: From molten rock to oceans, continents and mountains. When: 4.54 billion years ago.

passages.title: Chapter 9: Life from water
passages.text: Life from water: Life appears, the air fills with oxygen, and the land turns green. When: About 3.7 billion years ago.

passages.title: Chapter 10: The folding of the heavens
passages.text: The folding of the heavens: Possible futures, and a return. When: The end.

passages.title: Primordial deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio by number, D/H = (25.08 ± 0.29) × 10^-6: the PDG recommended value from quasar
passages.text: Primordial deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio by number, D/H = (25.08 ± 0.29) × 10^-6: the PDG recommended value from quasar: 0.000025 ± 0 (by number, relative to hydrogen). Source: Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, eq. (24.2).

passages.text: Primordial helium-4 mass fraction Y_P, inferred from metal-poor extragalactic H II regions; the PDG recommended value,: 0.245 ± 0.003 (primordial value inferred from observations). Source: Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026 (Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011), eq. (24.3).

passages.text: Fraction of primordial atoms that are helium, derived from Y_P = 0.245 ± 0.003: 0.0755 ± 0.0011 (derived from Y_P). Source: Derived from Y_P in Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, eq. (24.3), with NIST atomic masses.

passages.text: Primordial hydrogen mass fraction, derived as X = 1 − Y_P = 1 − 0.245 = 0.755: 0.755 ± 0.003 (derived as 1 − Y_P). Source: Derived from Y_P in Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, eq. (24.3).

passages.text: Factor by which the calculated (standard BBN) primordial lithium-7 abundance exceeds the value observed in old stars: 3.3 (approximate). Source: Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, Sec. 24.5.

passages.text: Primordial lithium-7-to-hydrogen ratio by number inferred from metal-poor halo stars, Li/H = (1.45 ± 0.25) × 10^-10, eq: 0 ± 0 (observed in old stars; regarded as a lower bound). Source: Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, eq. (24.4).

passages.text: Lithium-7-to-hydrogen ratio calculated from standard Big-Bang nucleosynthesis with the CMB baryon density, Li/H = (4.72: 0 ± 0 (standard BBN calculation). Source: Fields, Molaro & Sarkar, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis, Review 24 in PDG 2026, eq. (24.10).

passages.title: The heat capacity of the oceans' mixed layer, as a time in units of B
passages.text: The heat capacity of the oceans' mixed layer, as a time in units of B: 4.7 B years (a model parameter as the paper gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: North, Cahalan and Coakley 1981, Rev. Geophys. Space Phys. 19, 91, "Energy balance climate models" (notation table and section 2).

passages.title: The effective radiative forcing of doubling the air's carbon dioxide
passages.text: The effective radiative forcing of doubling the air's carbon dioxide: 3.93 ± 0.47 W/m^2 (IPCC AR6's assessment (likely range)). Source: Forster et al. 2021, in Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis (IPCC AR6 WG1), Chapter 7, executive summary: ERF for a doubling of CO2 3.93 +/- 0.47 W m-2.

passages.title: Temperature of the cosmic microwave background today, from the review of all published measurements in Fixsen (2009),
passages.text: Temperature of the cosmic microwave background today, from the review of all published measurements in Fixsen (2009),: 2.72548 ± 0.00057 K. Source: Fixsen 2009, ApJ 707, 916, abstract.

passages.text: Highest reported preference for evolving dark energy over a cosmological constant (DESI DR2 + CMB + supernovae): 4.2 σ (depends on the supernova sample; not a discovery). Source: DESI Collaboration 2025, Phys. Rev. D 112, 083515, "DESI DR2 Results II", abstract.

passages.title: Lowest reported preference for evolving dark energy over a cosmological constant (DESI DR2 + CMB + supernovae)
passages.text: Lowest reported preference for evolving dark energy over a cosmological constant (DESI DR2 + CMB + supernovae): 2.8 σ (depends on the supernova sample; not a discovery). Source: DESI Collaboration 2025, Phys. Rev. D 112, 083515, "DESI DR2 Results II", abstract.

passages.title: Age of the Earth
passages.text: Age of the Earth: 4.54 ± 0.05 Gyr (about 1% uncertainty; from the lead isotopes of ancient ores and meteorites). Source: Dalrymple 2001, Geological Society, London, Special Publications 190, 205, "The age of the Earth in the twentieth century: a problem (mostly) solved" (4.54 Ga, after Tera 1980).

passages.text: Height at which the night sky's green airglow, atomic oxygen's 557.7 nm line, is brightest: about 90 km over 10 to 20: 95 km (it varies with latitude and season (about 90 to 95 km in the cited measurements); the explorer draws the night side's airglow as one thin layer at this height). Source: Gao, H., Nee, J.-B. and Xu, J. 2012, "The emission of oxygen green line and density of O atom determined by using ISUAL and SABER measurements", Annales Geophysicae 30, 695-701.

passages.title: Argon in the Earth's dry air
passages.text: Argon in the Earth's dry air: 0.934 % by volume (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: argon 9340 ppm.

passages.title: Average temperature at the Earth's surface
passages.text: Average temperature at the Earth's surface: 15 °C (a global average (288 K); the fact sheet gives a diurnal range of 10 to 20 °C). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet, Terrestrial Atmosphere: average temperature 288 K (15 C).

passages.title: Carbon dioxide in the Earth's dry air
passages.text: Carbon dioxide in the Earth's dry air: 0.042 % by volume (as the fact sheet gives it; it rises year by year). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: carbon dioxide 420 ppm.

passages.title: Nitrogen in the Earth's dry air
passages.text: Nitrogen in the Earth's dry air: 78.08 % by volume (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: 78.08% nitrogen (N2).

passages.title: Oxygen in the Earth's dry air
passages.text: Oxygen in the Earth's dry air: 20.95 % by volume (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: 20.95% oxygen (O2).

passages.title: Scale height of the Earth's atmosphere: the height over which its pressure falls by a factor of e (about 2.7)
passages.text: Scale height of the Earth's atmosphere: the height over which its pressure falls by a factor of e (about 2.7): 8.5 km (approximate, for the lower atmosphere; it varies with temperature). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet, Terrestrial Atmosphere: scale height 8.5 km.

passages.title: Mean surface pressure of the Earth's atmosphere (sea level)
passages.text: Mean surface pressure of the Earth's atmosphere (sea level): 101.4 kPa (a global mean; weather moves it by a few per cent). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet, Terrestrial Atmosphere: surface pressure 1014 mb.

passages.title: The Earth's Bond albedo: the share of all sunlight it reflects
passages.text: The Earth's Bond albedo: the share of all sunlight it reflects: 0.294 dimensionless (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: Bond albedo 0.294.

passages.title: The mass of the Earth's water: oceans, ice and the rest
passages.text: The mass of the Earth's water: oceans, ice and the rest: 1,400,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: hydrosphere 1.4 x 10^21 kg.

passages.title: Earth's J2: the lowest zonal harmonic of its gravity field (its flattening's pull), normalised to its equatorial radius
passages.text: Earth's J2: the lowest zonal harmonic of its gravity field (its flattening's pull), normalised to its equatorial radius: 0.001083 dimensionless (as the fact sheet gives it (J2 x 10^-6)). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: J2 (x 10^-6) 1082.63.

passages.title: Earth's moment of inertia factor, I / (M R^2)
passages.text: Earth's moment of inertia factor, I / (M R^2): 0.3308 dimensionless (0.4 for a uniform sphere; lower the more its mass is held toward its centre). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: moment of inertia (I/MR^2) 0.3308.

passages.title: The share of the Earth's surface the ocean covers
passages.text: The share of the Earth's surface the ocean covers: 0.71 dimensionless (about 71 per cent). Source: NOAA, "How much water is in the ocean?": the ocean covers about 71 percent of the Earth's surface.

passages.title: Sunlight at the Earth's mean distance
passages.text: Sunlight at the Earth's mean distance: 1,361 W/m^2 (as the fact sheet gives it, without an uncertainty). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Earth Fact Sheet: solar irradiance 1361.0 W/m2.

passages.title: Cosmic age at z = 30 (first stars begin to form)
passages.text: Cosmic age at z = 30 (first stars begin to form): 99 Myr (derived from z = 30). Source: Derived with the Planck 2018 cosmology (astropy Planck18: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6, Table 2, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO) at z = 30.

passages.title: Cosmic age at z = 20 (Population III star formation well under way)
passages.text: Cosmic age at z = 20 (Population III star formation well under way): 178 Myr (derived from z = 20). Source: Derived with the Planck 2018 cosmology (astropy Planck18: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6, Table 2, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO) at z = 20.

passages.title: Redshift below which the first (Population III) stars form in current models
passages.text: Redshift below which the first (Population III) stars form in current models: 30 (about; model-dependent (Pop III stars form at z ≈ 30 and below)). Source: Klessen & Glover 2023, ARA&A 61, 65, "The first stars: formation, properties, and impact", abstract.

passages.title: Hubble constant from ACT DR6 + Planck + CMB lensing + DESI DR1 BAO
passages.text: Hubble constant from ACT DR6 + Planck + CMB lensing + DESI DR1 BAO: 68.22 ± 0.36 km/s/Mpc (early-universe inference, base ΛCDM). Source: Louis et al. 2025, "The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: DR6 Power Spectra, Likelihoods and ΛCDM Parameters", abstract.

passages.title: Hubble constant from the same combination with DESI DR2 BAO
passages.text: Hubble constant from the same combination with DESI DR2 BAO: 68.43 ± 0.27 km/s/Mpc (early-universe inference, base ΛCDM). Source: Louis et al. 2025, "The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: DR6 Power Spectra, Likelihoods and ΛCDM Parameters", abstract.

passages.title: Hubble constant from the Planck CMB, assuming base ΛCDM
passages.text: Hubble constant from the Planck CMB, assuming base ΛCDM: 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc (early-universe inference, base ΛCDM). Source: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6 (Planck 2018 results VI), abstract.

passages.title: Hubble constant measured locally by SH0ES (Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae)
passages.text: Hubble constant measured locally by SH0ES (Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae): 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc (local distance ladder). Source: Riess et al. 2022, ApJL 934, L7, "A Comprehensive Measurement of the Local Value of the Hubble Constant...", abstract.

passages.title: Statistical difference between the SH0ES value and the Planck + ΛCDM prediction
passages.text: Statistical difference between the SH0ES value and the Planck + ΛCDM prediction: 5 σ (as reported by SH0ES). Source: Riess et al. 2022, ApJL 934, L7, abstract ("a 5-sigma difference with H0 predicted by Planck+LCDM").

passages.title: Share of the iron in the universe made by Type Ia supernovae
passages.text: Share of the iron in the universe made by Type Ia supernovae: 0.5 (about half: Type Ia and core-collapse supernovae contributed roughly equally). Source: Maoz & Graur 2017, ApJ 848, 25, "Star formation, supernovae, iron, and α: consistent cosmic and Galactic histories", abstract.

passages.title: Jupiter's J2: the lowest zonal harmonic of its gravity field (its flattening's pull), normalised to its equatorial
passages.text: Jupiter's J2: the lowest zonal harmonic of its gravity field (its flattening's pull), normalised to its equatorial: 0.014736 dimensionless (as the fact sheet gives it (J2 x 10^-6)). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jupiter Fact Sheet: J2 (x 10^-6) 14736.

passages.title: Jupiter's moment of inertia factor, I / (M R^2)
passages.text: Jupiter's moment of inertia factor, I / (M R^2): 0.254 dimensionless (0.4 for a uniform sphere; lower the more its mass is held toward its centre). Source: D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jupiter Fact Sheet: moment of inertia (I/MR^2) 0.254.

passages.title: Cosmic age at the redshift of JADES-GS-z14-0
passages.text: Cosmic age at the redshift of JADES-GS-z14-0: 290 Myr (derived from z = 14.1793). Source: Derived with the Planck 2018 cosmology (astropy Planck18: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6, Table 2, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO) at z = 14.1793.

passages.title: Redshift of JADES-GS-z14-0 refined by ALMA

passages.title: Hot to cool
passages.text: As space stretched, everything in it cooled, from billions of degrees to about 3,000 kelvin some 380,000 years later, when the first light went free (Chapter 2).

passages.title: A point of light
passages.text: The film opens with a point of light. It is an illustration: the beginning was not an explosion at one place in space, and there was no outside to watch it from.

passages.title: Stretch space
passages.text: Hot and dense … Cooler and wider

passages.title: Space stretching
passages.text: The grains stand for matter spread through space. Nothing here flies apart through space: the space between the grains stretches, so every distance grows.

passages.title: The fog clears
passages.text: About 380,000 years after the beginning, at about 3,000 kelvin, electrons joined nuclei to make the first atoms. With nothing left to scatter it, light went straight on. That light still reaches us.

passages.title: The whole sky at once
passages.text: Seen from outside, the same map wraps a globe, the sky’s mirror image. Its faint patches are the seeds from which, through gravity, the galaxies grew.

passages.title: Which way the light vibrates
passages.text: This light is slightly polarised: it vibrates a little more in one direction than in others, set when it last bounced off electrons that saw a little more light from some sides than from others. The lines follow that direction as Planck measured it, smoothed to patterns a few degrees across. At that size the signal is still faint against Planck’s noise, so they show its best estimate, and they fade where the signal is weak and near our galaxy’s plane, whose own glow is in the way. Where each line starts, and how close the lines run, is only a way of drawing them.

passages.title: Inside the plasma
passages.text: Before the first light, the universe was a glowing fog of bare nuclei and free electrons. Light could not travel far without bouncing off an electron, so nothing could be seen through it.

passages.title: Let the first light go
passages.text: Opaque fog … Transparent: the first light

passages.title: The real sky of first light
passages.text: This is the Planck satellite’s map of that light, around you in its true directions. Its colours are tiny differences from an average of 2.7255 kelvin: blue a little colder, red a little warmer, by up to about 300 millionths of a degree.

passages.title: The dark ages
passages.text: After the first light, no star shone yet. Dark matter, shown in violet, was spread almost evenly, a little denser in some places than in others.

passages.title: The first galaxies
passages.text: The James Webb Space Telescope now sees galaxies from about 283 million years after the beginning, and today’s galaxy surveys measure the web itself.

passages.title: Let gravity work
passages.text: Nearly smooth … A web of galaxies

passages.title: The dark ages end
passages.text: The first stars’ ultraviolet light stripped the electrons from the hydrogen around them, and bubbles of ionised gas grew and merged. Planck measured how much of the first light those freed electrons scattered (an optical depth of 0.056): the gas was half ionised near redshift 7.8, about 657 million years after the beginning. The light of distant quasars shows its last neutral islands were gone by about redshift 5.3, around 1.1 billion years after it. The film shows only the start, far faster than it was; the bubbles are an illustration.

passages.title: The first stars
passages.text: The first stars lit in the knots, perhaps 99 to 178 million years after the beginning. None has been seen directly yet; these are illustrations.

passages.title: Gravity builds a web
passages.text: Gravity drew matter out of the thinner places into the denser ones, building sheets, threads and knots: the cosmic web. The film grows it with the Zel’dovich approximation, a simple model of that growth.

passages.title: Among the galaxies
passages.text: Galaxies scattered through space, each with billions of stars. They stand for the many galaxies whose light telescopes measure.

passages.title: Stretch space
passages.text: Before … Stretched and reddened

passages.title: Light reddens
passages.text: Light crossing stretching space is stretched with it: its waves lengthen and it shifts toward red. That redshift is measured for millions of galaxies.

passages.title: Space stretching
passages.text: As space stretches, the distances between galaxies grow, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster its distance grows. Edwin Hubble found that pattern in 1929.

passages.title: Two measurements disagree
passages.text: The expansion rate measured from the first light is about 67.4 km/s for every megaparsec of distance; measured from nearby stars and supernovae, about 73. The gap is real, at about 5 sigma, and still unexplained.

passages.title: Our galaxy
passages.text: The Milky Way, about 100,000 light-years across, with a few hundred billion stars. This is an artist’s model: no camera has seen our galaxy from outside.

passages.title: As far as we can see
passages.text: Light has had time to reach us from about 46.2 billion light-years away in every direction (farther than its travel time, because space stretched while it travelled). Beyond that, we cannot see.

passages.title: Draw back
passages.text: Our galaxy … Among the galaxies

passages.title: Drawing back
passages.text: Drawing back through five powers of ten, our galaxy becomes one point among many.

passages.title: Real galaxies
passages.text: These are 420,000 real galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, each at its measured position, out to light that left them about 7 billion years ago.

passages.title: The Sloan Great Wall
passages.text: One of the largest structures known: a wall of galaxies more than a billion light-years long, found in this survey’s maps in 2003.

passages.title: The core collapses
passages.text: Making iron gives no energy back, so when the iron core grows too heavy it collapses in under a second. Its rebound and a flood of neutrinos blow the star apart: a core-collapse supernova.

passages.title: Elements set free
passages.text: The debris carries elements made in the star and in the blast out into space, to become part of later stars, planets and living things.

passages.title: Burning in layers
passages.text: Near its end a massive star burns in shells, like an onion: hydrogen outside, then helium, carbon, oxygen, neon and silicon, around a core of iron. Not to scale.

passages.title: A massive star’s end
passages.text: Burning in layers … Elements scattered

passages.title: What the debris becomes
passages.text: An illustration: a composite after two real remnants. As in Cassiopeia A, the debris is far from a smooth shell. In places, plumes of iron have pushed out past the silicon that lay outside them in the star; a pair of opposite jets rich in silicon reaches out beyond the rest; and the inner debris is full of bubble-like cavities, which may have been opened by plumes of radioactive nickel-56, the nickel whose decay to iron this chapter follows. A faint rim marks the blast wave, running ahead into the gas around the star. At the centre is a neutron star (or, for the most massive stars, a black hole). Cassiopeia A’s neutron star has no glowing nebula round it: the faint glow here is borrowed from the Crab Nebula, where a young pulsar’s wind of particles lights the gas. The colours are the film’s own, one for each element, and the sizes are not to scale.

passages.title: A Type Ia supernova
passages.text: Near a critical mass it explodes completely. Its light then fades as nickel-56 decays to cobalt-56 (half-life 6.1 days) and cobalt-56 to iron (77 days). Such explosions made about half of the universe’s iron.

passages.title: A white dwarf and its companion
passages.text: A white dwarf, the Earth-sized core a smaller star leaves behind, draws gas from a companion star.

passages.title: A disk of dust
passages.text: The Sun and planets formed from a disk of gas and dust about 4.57 billion years ago. The gaps show where growing planets gathered material.

passages.title: The Sun’s course
passages.text: The Sun carries the planets around the centre of the Milky Way, once in about 230 million years. This is science, not the meaning of the verse.

passages.title: Jets of a young star
passages.text: A young star still gathering gas from its disk, as the Sun is thought to have done, drives two narrow jets out along its poles at a few hundred kilometres a second. Where faster gas catches up with slower, and where the jets plough into the cloud around them, the gas is shocked and glows red, in knots and bow-shaped fronts. The star’s light escapes through funnels the outflow has cleared in the dust. The James Webb Space Telescope has imaged both: the jets of HH 211 and the hourglass of L1527 (NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI). Shown here short and not to scale: real jets can stretch for light-years.

passages.title: The Moon’s phases
passages.text: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it circles the Earth we see more or less of that lit half: new, crescent, half, gibbous and full.

passages.title: Real orbits, today
passages.text: The planets on their orbits from NASA JPL’s orbital elements, at their positions for today’s date. Sizes and distances are not to scale.

passages.title: Let the planets move
passages.text: Now … Months later

passages.title: The living Sun
passages.text: The Sun’s surface: granulation (the tops of rising currents of hot gas), its darker edge, and the faint corona around it. Its surface is about 5,772 kelvin.

passages.title: Land rises
passages.text: Plates of crust move, continents and mountains rise, and clouds form in the new air.

passages.title: A giant impact
passages.text: A body about the size of Mars, often called Theia, struck the young Earth some 30 to 100 million years after the solar system formed. This is the leading explanation of the Moon, not a certainty.

passages.title: A molten world
passages.text: The young Earth, about 4.54 billion years ago: its surface molten from the heat of its forming and of constant impacts.

passages.title: The Moon gathers
passages.text: The debris thrown out by the impact gathered into the Moon, then much closer to the Earth than it is now.

passages.title: Rain and the first seas
passages.text: As the Earth cooled, water vapour fell as rain, filling the first oceans. Tiny zircon crystals suggest there was liquid water by about 4.4 billion years ago.

passages.title: Shape the young Earth
passages.text: Molten … Seas and land

passages.title: The land turns green
passages.text: Plants spread over the land in the last half-billion years, changing the colour of the continents.

passages.title: The early ocean
passages.text: Light filtering through the early ocean. The oldest widely accepted traces of life are about 3.5 billion years old: single cells. How life began is not known; this is not a reconstruction of it.

passages.title: Oxygen in the air
passages.text: From about 2.43 billion years ago, microbes making oxygen slowly changed the air (the Great Oxidation Event), and the sea and the sky changed with it.

passages.title: Let the Earth change
passages.text: A water world … A living Earth

passages.title: Up through the surface
passages.text: Rising out of the sea to see the whole Earth.

passages.title: Big Crunch (a model)
passages.text: If expansion reversed, everything could fall back together. Today’s measurements do not favour it.

passages.title: Big Rip (a model)
passages.text: If dark energy grows stronger, expansion could one day pull galaxies, stars and even atoms apart. Another hypothesis.

passages.title: Heat death (a model)
passages.text: If expansion goes on as now, stars will burn out and the universe will grow cold and dark over immense spans of time. This is one hypothesis.

passages.title: The cosmos today
passages.text: Galaxies today. Space is still stretching, and since 1998 we have known that the stretching is speeding up.

passages.title: Explore Mode: The map and how it was measured
passages.text: Measured by ESA’s Planck satellite between 2009 and 2013; this is its 2018 map made by the SMICA method, which separates the first light from the light of our own galaxy. Its finest details are about a twelfth of a degree across, a sixth of the full Moon’s width. Along the band where our galaxy shines brightest, the map is a careful reconstruction rather than a direct view. Our own motion makes one half of the sky about 3 thousandths of a degree warmer; that effect has been taken out.

passages.title: Explore Mode: The Earth today
passages.text: The young Earth here is a model. The solar system explorer shows the real Earth now: its clouds, its night side and the satellites around it. A day lasts 24 hours now. Soon after the Moon formed it was much shorter, and the Moon’s pull is still slowing the Earth, by about 2 thousandths of a second a century.

passages.title: Explore Mode: Expanding space: a model
passages.text: The dots stand in for galaxies. Stretch the space between them and watch the distances from the dot you choose. Choose any dot: from every one, all the others move away, the farther ones faster. No dot is the centre. A model, not a picture of the beginning.

passages.title: Explore Mode: Models, not the unseen
passages.text: These are scientific models of how the universe might end, each a hypothesis that measurements could rule out. The Quran’s descriptions of the Last Day speak of the unseen; the film does not picture them, and these models are not their depiction.

passages.title: Explore Mode: Kepler’s law, from the real orbits
passages.text: A planet’s year grows with its distance from the Sun: the square of the year follows the cube of the distance. Choose a planet.

passages.title: Explore Mode: Stretch space
passages.text: Galaxies are not flying through space: the space between them grows, and light crossing it is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths.

passages.title: Explore Mode: Two kinds of supernova
passages.text: A star of more than about eight times the Sun’s mass A white dwarf in a pair of stars It gains mass until its carbon fuses in a runaway Shows hydrogen; its brightness varies No hydrogen; nearly the same peak brightness every time Spreads oxygen and many other elements A measuring stick for distance: it showed in 1998 that expansion is speeding up

passages.title: Explore Mode: Why water matters
passages.text: At the pressure of our air, water stays liquid from 0 to 100 °C, the range most life on Earth depends on. Ice floats: water is densest at about 4 °C, so lakes and seas freeze from the top down and life goes on below. Water holds heat well, so the oceans steady the climate. It dissolves many substances, carrying what cells need. Where liquid water can last on a planet’s surface depends on its distance from its star and on its air: the habitable zone. It is a condition for life as we know it, not a sign of life.

passages.title: Sunan Abi Dawud 4700
passages.text: Sunan Abi Dawud 4700, narrated by Ubadah ibn as-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by al-Albani. A summary, not a quotation: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ tells that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, and that it was commanded to write. On its grading: The same hadith of the Pen in Jami at-Tirmidhi 2155 is noted by at-Tirmidhi as gharib by its chain. Both gradings are shown together.

passages.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3191
passages.text: Sahih al-Bukhari 3191, narrated by Imran ibn Husain (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by al-Bukhari, by its inclusion in Sahih al-Bukhari. A summary, not a quotation: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ speaks of Allah (glorified and exalted is He) existing when nothing else existed. He speaks of His Throne being over the water, of His writing all things in the Dhikr, and of His creating the heavens and the earth.

passages.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 3199
passages.text: Sahih al-Bukhari 3199, narrated by Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by al-Bukhari, by its inclusion in Sahih al-Bukhari. A summary, not a quotation: Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said the sun goes, at its setting, to prostrate beneath the Throne, and asks permission to rise again.

passages.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 4812
passages.text: Sahih al-Bukhari 4812, narrated by Abu Huraira (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by al-Bukhari, by its inclusion in Sahih al-Bukhari. A summary, not a quotation: Abu Huraira (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection Allah (glorified and exalted is He) will grasp the earth and roll up the heavens.

passages.title: Sahih Muslim 2653
passages.text: Sahih Muslim 2653, narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by Muslim, by its inclusion in Sahih Muslim. A summary, not a quotation: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ tells that the measures of creation were written fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth were created, while His Throne was over the water.

passages.title: Sahih Muslim 2787
passages.text: Sahih Muslim 2787, narrated by Abu Huraira (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Sahih by Muslim, by its inclusion in Sahih Muslim. A summary, not a quotation: Abu Huraira (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection Allah (glorified and exalted is He) will grasp the earth and roll up the heavens.

passages.title: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2155
passages.text: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2155, narrated by Ubadah ibn as-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him). Graded Gharib (by this chain) by at-Tirmidhi. A summary, not a quotation: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ tells that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, and that it was commanded to write. On its grading: At-Tirmidhi notes that this hadith is gharib by this chain. The same hadith of the Pen in Sunan Abi Dawud 4700 is graded sahih by al-Albani; both gradings are shown together.

passages.title: In plain words: absolute magnitude
passages.text: How bright the star would look if every star were set at the same distance. The smaller the number, the brighter the star really shines.

passages.title: In plain words: add body
passages.text: Add a new moon, planet or star to the experiment, and see how everything else responds.

passages.title: In plain words: apparent magnitude
passages.text: How bright the star looks from the Earth. The smaller the number, the brighter it looks: on a dark night the faintest stars you can see are about 6.

passages.title: In plain words: apsides
passages.text: The nearest and farthest points of an orbit. Most orbits are stretched circles, so a world comes closer and goes farther as it travels.

passages.title: In plain words: asr
passages.text: Asr, the afternoon prayer, begins when a stick’s shadow has grown longer than it was at midday: by the stick’s own length in one way of counting, by twice its length in another.

passages.title: In plain words: astrolabe
passages.text: An astrolabe is an old instrument that shows the sky on a flat plate. Astronomers in the Islamic world used it to tell the time and find the stars. This one shows the sky for your place right now.

passages.title: In plain words: atlas
passages.text: A tour of amazing places on the Earth, like great canyons, volcanoes and reefs. Tap Go to fly to one.

passages.title: In plain words: autopilot
passages.text: The autopilot works out the burns for you, using the same rocket rules. It can only do what the fuel allows.

passages.title: In plain words: Earth
passages.text: The Earth is our home: a rocky planet with air we can breathe and oceans of water. It is the only place we know of that has life.

passages.title: In plain words: Jupiter
passages.text: Jupiter is the biggest planet. It is made mostly of gas, so there is no solid ground to stand on, and its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the Earth.

passages.title: In plain words: Mars
passages.text: Mars is a rocky planet about half as wide as the Earth. Its red colour comes from rusty dust, and it has the tallest volcano we know of, Olympus Mons.

passages.title: In plain words: Mercury
passages.text: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no air, so its days are scorching and its nights are freezing.

passages.title: In plain words: Moon
passages.text: The Moon travels around the Earth about once a month. It has no air and no light of its own: it shines because sunlight bounces off it.

passages.title: In plain words: Neptune
passages.text: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. It is an icy giant with the fastest winds of any planet.

passages.title: In plain words: Saturn
passages.text: Saturn is a giant planet made mostly of gas, famous for its rings. The rings are countless pieces of ice and rock, all travelling around the planet.

passages.title: In plain words: Sun
passages.text: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of very hot, glowing gas. About a million Earths could fit inside it, and its light and warmth keep us alive.

passages.title: In plain words: Uranus
passages.text: Uranus is an icy giant planet. It is tipped over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.

passages.title: In plain words: Venus
passages.text: Venus is about the size of the Earth, but it is wrapped in thick clouds. Its air traps so much heat that it is the hottest planet, hotter even than Mercury.

passages.title: In plain words: breakup
passages.text: If it spun faster than this, the spinning would fling it apart, because its own gravity could no longer hold it together.

passages.title: In plain words: burn
passages.text: Which way the rocket pushes: forward along the path (prograde) makes the orbit bigger, backwards (retrograde) makes it smaller, and sideways tips it or changes its shape.

passages.title: In plain words: camera
passages.text: Settings for your picture: how wide the view is (the lens) and how bright it is (the exposure). You can also keep another world in the same place in the frame as time runs.

passages.title: In plain words: checks
passages.text: These numbers check that the simulation is working properly. Energy and momentum should stay the same unless you change something.

passages.title: In plain words: climate
passages.text: How warm this world would be, worked out from its sunlight and its air. It is a simple model: it shows the big picture, not the weather.

passages.title: In plain words: convention
passages.text: Each organisation has its own rule for working out prayer times. They differ mostly in how far below the horizon the Sun must be for the dawn and night prayers.

passages.title: In plain words: cosmic web
passages.text: Galaxies are not spread out evenly. They gather along huge threads and walls with great empty spaces between, like a web. These dots are real galaxies a survey measured.

passages.title: In plain words: crescent map
passages.text: This map shows where on the Earth the thin new crescent might be seen after sunset, from easily (green) to not at all (red). It shows what the sky allows, not when anyone’s month begins.

passages.title: In plain words: criterion
passages.text: Astronomers have made tests, from many real sightings, to judge whether a new crescent can be seen. Yallop’s and Odeh’s are two of them, and you can compare them.

passages.title: In plain words: day
passages.text: A day is how long a world takes to spin around once. Here there are two: one full spin, and the time from one sunrise to the next, which can be quite different.

passages.title: In plain words: delta v
passages.text: Delta-v means “change in speed”. It tells you how much more speed the ship’s fuel can still give it.

passages.title: In plain words: density
passages.text: Density is how tightly packed something is: a stone is denser than a sponge of the same size. Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant bath of water!

passages.title: In plain words: descent
passages.text: Ride down through the clouds the way a real space probe did. The numbers on the way down are the ones that probe measured.

passages.title: In plain words: descent air
passages.text: How hard the air presses, how hot it is, and how thick it is at this height. Deep in Venus’s air it presses as hard as the sea does nearly a kilometre down.

passages.title: In plain words: descent probe
passages.text: These numbers were measured by a real probe that fell through these clouds, sending them home by radio as it went.

passages.title: In plain words: detail
passages.text: How much detail the explorer draws. More detail looks sharper but needs a faster device. Auto picks what suits yours.

passages.title: In plain words: distance
passages.text: How far away each world is from you. An AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.

passages.title: In plain words: eccentricity
passages.text: How stretched an orbit is: 0 is a perfect circle, and the closer to 1, the longer and thinner the oval.

passages.title: In plain words: elements
passages.text: These numbers describe an orbit: how big it is, how stretched and how tipped. Change them to put the body on a different path.

passages.title: In plain words: escape
passages.text: Escape speed is how fast you would have to throw something straight up for it never to fall back. The stronger a world’s gravity, the faster you have to go.

passages.title: In plain words: exoplanets
passages.text: Exoplanets are planets that go around other stars. Most are too faint to see: astronomers find them by the tiny wobble or dimming they cause in their star.

passages.title: In plain words: field notes
passages.text: These are interesting places and things Samee wants to show you on the Earth. You can learn about them and visit the places in the explorer.

passages.title: In plain words: find place
passages.text: Type the name of a town or city, then choose it to fly there.

passages.title: In plain words: fixed
passages.text: Hold this body still, as if it were pinned in place, to see what happens to the others. Real worlds can’t be held still: this is a thought experiment.

passages.title: In plain words: frame
passages.text: Choose how paths are drawn: around each world, as seen from far away, or turning along with a world. The motion is the same; only the view changes.

passages.title: In plain words: from sun
passages.text: How far this world is from the Sun right now. Orbits are slightly stretched circles, so this distance changes a little through its year.

passages.title: In plain words: galaxy type
passages.text: Galaxies come in different shapes: spirals like giant whirlpools, round or oval ones called ellipticals, and irregular ones with no clear shape.

passages.title: In plain words: golden
passages.text: The golden ratio is a special number, about 1.618, found in some shapes in nature and art. This shows how close the Kaaba’s latitude comes to the place that splits the way between the poles in that ratio: a closeness of numbers, not a proof of anything.

passages.title: In plain words: graph
passages.text: Follow a number over time, like a distance or a speed, as a line on a chart.

passages.title: In plain words: gravity
passages.text: Gravity is an invisible pull between things. It’s why you stay on the ground and why planets travel around the Sun. This number is how strong the pull is at the surface.

passages.title: In plain words: greenhouse
passages.text: Some gases in the air trap heat like a blanket. More of them makes a world warmer.

passages.title: In plain words: heritage
passages.text: Places where great astronomers and mathematicians of the Islamic world lived and worked. Tap Go to visit them.

passages.title: In plain words: hijri
passages.text: This is the date in the Islamic calendar, which follows the Moon: each month is about one Moon cycle. This one is worked out the way Saudi Arabia’s Umm al-Qura calendar does it.

passages.title: In plain words: hill
passages.text: The space around a world where its own gravity wins over the Sun’s, so moons can stay with it.

passages.title: In plain words: history
passages.text: Every change you make is listed here. You can go back to an earlier moment and try something different.

passages.title: In plain words: hr
passages.text: Each dot is a star, placed by its colour (left to right) and how brightly it really shines (up and down). Stars of the same kind gather together, like the long band where most stars, the Sun among them, are found.

passages.title: In plain words: imagery
passages.text: Choose the picture of the Earth: a clear one with no clouds, made from many photos, or today’s photo with today’s real clouds.

passages.title: In plain words: inclination
passages.text: How tipped an orbit is compared with others, like a tilted hula hoop.

passages.title: In plain words: islamic
passages.text: The Sun and the Moon help Muslims find the direction of prayer, the times of prayer and the start of each month. This section works these out with the explorer’s own astronomy.

passages.title: In plain words: j2
passages.text: How squashed a spinning world is. Fast-spinning worlds bulge out a little around their middle.

passages.title: In plain words: kaaba sun
passages.text: Twice a year the Sun passes straight overhead at the Kaaba. At that moment the shadow of anything standing upright in the sunlit half of the world points away from the qibla, so a stick can show the way.

passages.title: In plain words: lab
passages.text: This is where you can ask “What if?” about space. Change things like a planet’s mass or speed and see what the science models say would happen. It is a copy of the solar system: the real one is never changed.

passages.title: In plain words: lab bodies
passages.text: Everything in this experiment. Choose one to see its numbers and change them, and tick several to follow them together.

passages.title: In plain words: lab clock
passages.text: The laboratory’s own clock. Speed it up to see orbits and changes happen faster, or pause it to change things carefully.

passages.title: In plain words: lab slow
passages.text: When something is about to hit something else, or a moon is about to be torn apart, the laboratory’s clock slows down so you can watch it, then speeds up again. The physics is the same at any speed. Turn it off to keep your own speed.

passages.title: In plain words: lab throw
passages.text: Aim a rock at a world. The laboratory works out where it must start so it strikes how and when you asked, shows you what will happen, and only then lets you throw it.

passages.title: In plain words: lessons
passages.text: Short guided experiments that show one idea at a time, with the number science expects beside the number the experiment gives.

passages.title: In plain words: light time
passages.text: Light is very fast, but space is enormous! This tells you how long light takes to reach you from each world. So looking far into space is also looking into the past.

passages.title: In plain words: light year
passages.text: A light year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.5 million million kilometres. A parsec is about 3.26 light years.

passages.title: In plain words: living
passages.text: The real Earth, live: today’s pictures from space, satellites going around it, and recent earthquakes. Turn on what you would like to see.

passages.title: In plain words: local group
passages.text: The Milky Way has neighbours: the Andromeda Galaxy and many smaller galaxies. Together they are called the Local Group.

passages.title: In plain words: luminosity
passages.text: How much light a star gives out in every direction, compared with the Sun.

passages.title: In plain words: mass
passages.text: Mass is how much stuff something is made of. A world with more mass pulls harder with its gravity.

passages.title: In plain words: measure
passages.text: Measure the distance between two objects, how long light takes to cross it, and the angle between them.

passages.title: In plain words: milky way
passages.text: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a huge spinning disc of hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is one of them. This is a model of its shape, built from measurements.

passages.title: In plain words: navigator
passages.text: This is your guide to space. Tap a world to fly there, and open the sections below to learn about it and try things out.

passages.title: In plain words: new moon
passages.text: At new moon the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away and we can’t see it. A day or so later a thin crescent may appear after sunset, and many communities begin each Islamic month when it is seen.

passages.title: In plain words: orbit
passages.text: An orbit is the path something follows as it travels around another object. The Earth travels around the Sun, and the Moon travels around the Earth.

passages.title: In plain words: orrery
passages.text: A little map of the solar system seen from above, with the Sun in the middle. The directions are real for the date shown, but the distances are squeezed so everything fits.

passages.title: In plain words: parallax
passages.text: Telescopes find a star’s distance by watching it shift a tiny bit as the Earth goes around the Sun. It is like the way your finger seems to jump when you look at it with one eye and then the other.

passages.title: In plain words: period
passages.text: How long one trip around its orbit takes.

passages.title: In plain words: photo
passages.text: Photo mode hides the buttons so you see only the view. You can save a picture or a video, with a note underneath of where its pictures and numbers came from.

passages.title: In plain words: prayer times
passages.text: Muslims pray five times a day, at times set by where the Sun is in the sky: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. Different organisations use slightly different rules, so you can choose one.

passages.title: In plain words: prediction
passages.text: The path drawn ahead is worked out by the computer from the same rules, a little way into the future. It is a calculation, not a certainty.

passages.title: In plain words: prophets
passages.text: Places on the Earth linked by tradition to the lives of the prophets, peace be upon them. Where traditions disagree about a place, no pin is shown.

passages.title: In plain words: push
passages.text: A push changes how fast something moves and which way. A push along its path makes its orbit bigger, and a push against its path makes it smaller.

passages.title: In plain words: qibla
passages.text: The qibla is the direction Muslims face when they pray: towards the Kaaba in Makkah. Here it is the shortest path over the round Earth, measured from true north.

passages.title: In plain words: quakes
passages.text: An earthquake is when the ground suddenly shakes, because huge pieces of the Earth’s outer layer slip past each other. These marks show recent ones.

passages.title: In plain words: radius
passages.text: The radius is the distance from the middle of a ball to its outside. A bigger radius means a bigger world.

passages.title: In plain words: rings
passages.text: Add a ring or belt of tiny pieces around a world and watch how gravity moves them.

passages.title: In plain words: roche
passages.text: If a moon comes closer than this to its planet, the planet’s pull is stronger on its near side than its far side and can pull it apart.

passages.title: In plain words: rotation
passages.text: How fast it spins, and how far its axis leans compared with its orbit.

passages.title: In plain words: satellites
passages.text: Satellites are machines people have sent up to travel around the Earth. Some take pictures, and some help phones and maps work.

passages.title: In plain words: saved
passages.text: Save the view you have now, with its place and date, so you can come back to it. Saved views stay in this browser only.

passages.title: In plain words: seen
passages.text: Special things you have noticed on this visit, like Jupiter’s squashed shape. It is just a list for you, not a score.

passages.title: In plain words: semi major
passages.text: Half the longest width of an oval orbit: a way of saying how big the orbit is.

passages.title: In plain words: ship
passages.text: A spaceship with a rocket engine. Its fuel is limited, so every burn of the engine uses some of it up.

passages.title: In plain words: sky
passages.text: Lines and names you can add to the sky: the star patterns people have long known (constellations), their borders, and a grid that helps find places on the sky.

passages.title: In plain words: sound
passages.text: You hear the wind where there is air, like when you walk on the Earth or Mars. Where there is no air you only hear your space suit, because sound can’t travel through empty space. This also turns the film’s sounds on or off.

passages.title: In plain words: spectral type
passages.text: A star’s type tells you how hot it is and what colour it shines, from hot blue-white stars to cool red ones. The Sun is a yellow-white star of type G.

passages.title: In plain words: speed
passages.text: How fast it is moving, and how fast compared with the world it travels around.

passages.title: In plain words: spin
passages.text: How fast the world turns, and how much its axis leans.

passages.title: In plain words: stars
passages.text: Travel past the planets to the stars around the Sun. Each star is placed where telescopes measured it to be.

passages.title: In plain words: stars search
passages.text: Type a star’s name, like Sirius, or its catalogue number, then choose it to fly there.

passages.title: In plain words: sunlight
passages.text: How much light from its star lands here, compared with how much reaches the Earth.

passages.title: In plain words: temperature
passages.text: How hot the star’s glowing surface is, in kelvin (degrees above the coldest possible). The Sun’s surface is about 5,800 kelvin.

passages.title: In plain words: tilt
passages.text: A world spins around a line called its axis. When the axis leans over, each half of the world gets more sunlight at a different time of year, and that makes the seasons.

passages.title: In plain words: time
passages.text: These buttons change time in the explorer: speed it up to watch the planets move, slow it down, run it backwards, pause it, or pick a date between 1600 and 2399. Outside JPL’s tables the Moon and planets come from published formulas, a little less exact. In an experiment they run its own clock, and backwards replays its history.

passages.title: In plain words: today
passages.text: What is happening on the Earth right now: where the Sun is overhead, where the day is starting and ending, and where the space station is.

passages.title: In plain words: tour
passages.text: Fly from one saved view to the next, like a little film. Record a video while it plays!

passages.title: In plain words: walk
passages.text: Put on a space suit and walk on the ground! The shape of the ground comes from real measurements made by spacecraft.

passages.title: In plain words: walk air
passages.text: Air pressure is how hard the air above you presses down. On Mars the air is very thin, and on Venus it presses about 90 times harder than on the Earth.

passages.title: In plain words: walk gravity
passages.text: How strongly you are pulled down here. On the Moon it is about a sixth of the Earth’s, so you could jump much higher.

passages.title: In plain words: walk ground
passages.text: How high the ground is compared with the world’s “sea level”. On worlds with no seas, scientists choose a level to measure from instead.

passages.title: In plain words: walk qibla
passages.text: The direction of the qibla from where you are standing, and how far to turn to face it.

passages.title: In plain words: walk sun
passages.text: How high the Sun is in the sky, and the time a sundial here would show.

passages.title: In plain words: year
passages.text: A year is how long a world takes to travel once around the Sun. Worlds farther from the Sun have longer years.

passages.text: This narration and Jami at-Tirmidhi 2155 are together known as the hadith of the Pen.

passages.title: Chapter 0: Before creation: a note on 36:82
passages.text: The single word shown in calligraphy in this chapter is taken from the Tanzil text of this verse and set in the Amiri Quran typeface.

passages.title: Chapter 2: The first light: a note on 41:11
passages.text: This chapter does not identify the smoke in this verse with the glowing plasma of the early universe or with the microwave background shown in the scene.

passages.title: Chapter 3: The dark ages and first stars: a note on How scholars have understood it
passages.text: With no verse in this chapter, there is no scholarly reading to summarise.

passages.title: Chapter 3: The dark ages and first stars: a note on What the text says
passages.text: No verse is placed beside this chapter. The science stands here on its own, between the passages before it and after it.

passages.title: Chapter 6: Stars and iron: a note on 39:6
passages.text: Shown for comparison: here the same verb, anzala (“sent down”), is used of livestock.

passages.title: Chapter 7: The Sun and its course: a note on bukhari-3199
passages.text: A matter of the unseen (ghayb), not a physical claim about orbits. Scholars have read it in different ways.

passages.title: Chapter 8: The earth spread out: a note on 22:47
passages.text: Context: people were asking for the promised punishment to be hastened.

passages.title: Chapter 8: The earth spread out: a note on 70:4
passages.text: Context: this verse concerns the ascent of the angels and the Spirit.

passages.text: This speaks of the unseen. Nothing in this film pictures it.

passages.title: Adam, peace be upon him: Adam’s Peak (Sri Pada), Sri Lanka
passages.text: By tradition, the first human and the first prophet. Early Muslim histories record that he came down to Earth in Sarandib, the island now called Sri Lanka. Muslims have long linked him with the mountain there called Adam’s Peak, marked here; it is holy to other faiths too. These reports are weakly attested, and others name other places.

passages.title: Al-Yasa (Elisha), peace be upon him
passages.text: By tradition, he succeeded Ilyas. Where he lived is not known, so no place is marked.

passages.title: Ayyub (Job), peace be upon him
passages.text: Remembered for his patience. Traditions differ about where he lived (among them the Hauran in Syria and near Salalah in Oman), so no place is marked.

passages.title: Dawud (David), peace be upon him: Jerusalem (al-Quds)
passages.text: By tradition, a prophet and a king, who ruled from Jerusalem.

passages.title: Dhul-Kifl, peace be upon him
passages.text: Little is narrated of his life, and traditions differ about who and where he was, so no place is marked.

passages.title: Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him: Jabal Harun, by Petra
passages.text: By tradition, his brother Musa’s helper, he died during their journey through the wilderness. Jabal Harun, by Petra in Jordan, is held by tradition to be where he is buried.

passages.title: Hud, peace be upon him: Shib Hud, Hadramawt
passages.text: By tradition, sent to the people of ’Ad in southern Arabia. A tomb in the Hadramawt valley of Yemen is held by local tradition to be his, and is marked here.

passages.title: Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him: Harran, Hebron (al-Khalil), Makkah
passages.text: By tradition, he left Mesopotamia, by way of Harran in today’s Türkiye, for the land of Canaan. With his son Ismail he raised the House at Makkah, and he is buried at Hebron, whose Arabic name, al-Khalil, is his.

passages.title: Idris, peace be upon him
passages.text: Little is narrated of his life. Some traditions place him in Babylon and in Egypt; none is certain, so no place is marked.

passages.title: Ilyas (Elijah), peace be upon him
passages.text: By tradition, he called his people away from the worship of Baal. Where he preached is not certain, so no place is marked.

passages.title: Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him: Nazareth, Jerusalem (al-Quds)
passages.text: By tradition, the son of Maryam, he grew up in Nazareth, in Galilee, and taught in Jerusalem and the lands around it.

passages.title: Ishaq (Isaac), peace be upon him: Hebron (al-Khalil)
passages.text: By tradition, he lived in the land of Canaan and is buried at Hebron, beside his father.

passages.title: Ismail (Ishmael), peace be upon him: Makkah
passages.text: By tradition, brought as an infant with his mother Hajar to the valley of Makkah, where he grew up and, with his father, raised the House.

passages.title: Lut (Lot), peace be upon him: The Dead Sea
passages.text: By tradition, sent to the towns of the plain beside the Dead Sea. Where those towns stood is not known; the sea itself is marked.

passages.title: Muhammad ﷺ: Makkah, Madinah
passages.text: Born in Makkah, where the revelation began; he migrated to Madinah, where he is buried.

passages.title: Musa (Moses), peace be upon him: Jabal Musa, Sinai
passages.text: By tradition, raised in Egypt, he led his people out and was spoken to at the mountain. Many identify it with Jabal Musa in Sinai, marked here; others name other mountains.

passages.title: Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him: Mount Judi
passages.text: By tradition, the ark came to rest on al-Judi. Many identify it with Mount Judi in south-east Türkiye, marked here; others name other mountains.

passages.title: Salih, peace be upon him: Hegra (al-Hijr)
passages.text: By tradition, sent to the people of Thamud, who carved their homes from the rock. Tradition places them at al-Hijr, by Hegra in north-west Arabia, marked here; the tombs seen there now were cut later, by the Nabataeans.

passages.title: Shuayb, peace be upon him: Al-Bad (Madyan)
passages.text: By tradition, sent to the people of Madyan, usually placed in north-west Arabia by the Gulf of Aqaba. The oasis of al-Bad, long identified with Madyan, is marked here.

passages.title: Sulayman (Solomon), peace be upon him: Jerusalem (al-Quds)
passages.text: By tradition, he succeeded his father Dawud as king and ruled from Jerusalem.

passages.title: Yahya (John), peace be upon him: The Umayyad Mosque, Damascus
passages.text: By tradition, the son of Zakariyya. A shrine in the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus is associated with him, and is marked here; traditions differ about where he is buried.

passages.title: Yaqub (Jacob), peace be upon him: Hebron (al-Khalil)
passages.text: By tradition, he lived in Canaan, came to Egypt late in life to be with Yusuf, and was buried at Hebron.

passages.title: Yunus (Jonah), peace be upon him: Nineveh, by Mosul
passages.text: By tradition, sent to Nineveh, on the Tigris by today’s Mosul in Iraq, whose people turned back to faith.

passages.title: Yusuf (Joseph), peace be upon him: Bahr Yussef, Fayum
passages.text: By tradition, sold into Egypt as a boy, he came to oversee its stores. A branch of the Nile in the Fayum, Bahr Yussef, carries his name, and is marked here.

passages.title: Zakariyya (Zechariah), peace be upon him: Jerusalem (al-Quds)
passages.text: By tradition, he served in the house of worship at Jerusalem and was the guardian of Maryam.

passages.title: 14:48 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: On that Day the earth will be changed into a different earth, and the heavens too, and everyone will come out before Allah, the One, the All-Powerful.

passages.title: 21:104 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: On that Day We will roll up the sky as a written scroll is rolled up. Just as We began the first creation, We will bring it back again: a promise binding on Us, and We will surely carry it out.

passages.title: 21:30 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Do those who reject faith not see that the heavens and the earth were once joined together, and that We split them apart? And We made every living thing from water. Will they still not believe?

passages.title: 21:33 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He is the One who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon, each moving along in its own orbit.

passages.title: 22:47 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: They ask you to hurry on the punishment, but Allah never breaks His promise. A day with your Lord is like a thousand years as you count them.

passages.title: 24:45 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Allah created every creature from water. Some of them crawl on their bellies, some walk on two legs and some on four. Allah creates whatever He wills; He has power over everything.

passages.title: 25:59 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six Days, then rose above the Throne: the Most Merciful. Ask about Him one who truly knows.

passages.title: 2:117 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He brought the heavens and the earth into being when nothing like them existed. When He decides on something, He only says to it, “Be!”, and it is.

passages.title: 32:4 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six Days, then rose above the Throne. Apart from Him you have no protector and no one to plead for you. Will you not take heed?

passages.title: 32:5 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He directs every matter from the heavens to the earth; then it rises back up to Him in a Day whose length is a thousand years as you count them.

passages.title: 36:38 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: And the sun runs on to its appointed resting place. That is the plan of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.

passages.title: 36:39 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: And for the moon We have set stages, until it becomes again like an old, dried, curved palm stalk.

passages.title: 36:40 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: The sun cannot overtake the moon, and the night cannot get ahead of the day: each is moving along in its own orbit.

passages.title: 36:82 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: When He wills something, His only command is to say to it, “Be!”, and it is.

passages.title: 39:6 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He created you all from a single soul, then made its mate from it, and He provided you with eight kinds of livestock in pairs. He forms you in your mothers’ wombs, stage after stage, within three layers of darkness. That is Allah, your Lord; the kingdom is His. There is no god but Him, so how can you turn away?

passages.title: 39:67 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: They have not valued Allah as He truly deserves. On the Day of Resurrection the whole earth will be within His grasp, and the heavens rolled up in His right hand. Glorified and exalted is He above the partners they claim for Him.

passages.title: 41:10 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He placed firm mountains on it, standing high above it, blessed it, and measured out its provisions in four Days, the same for all who ask.

passages.title: 41:11 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth, “Come, willingly or unwillingly.” They said, “We come willingly.”

passages.title: 41:12 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: So He made them seven heavens in two Days, and gave each heaven its command. We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and kept it guarded. That is the plan of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.

passages.title: 41:9 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Say: Do you really reject the One who created the earth in two Days, and set up rivals to Him? He is the Lord of all the worlds.

passages.title: 50:38 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: We created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six Days, and no tiredness touched Us.

passages.title: 51:47 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: We built the heaven with strength, and it is We who give it its vastness.

passages.title: 55:33 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: O jinn and humans, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass beyond them! You cannot, except with authority from Allah.

passages.title: 57:25 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: We sent Our messengers with clear signs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the Balance, so that people would uphold justice. And We sent down iron, with its great strength and many benefits for people, so that Allah might make known who supports Him and His messengers without seeing Him. Allah is Strong and Almighty.

passages.title: 65:12 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Allah is the One who created seven heavens, and of the earth the like of them. His command comes down through them all, so that you may know that Allah has power over everything and that His knowledge encompasses all things.

passages.title: 67:3 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: He created seven heavens, one above another. You will see no flaw in what the Most Merciful creates. Look again: can you see any cracks?

passages.title: 70:4 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: The angels and the Spirit rise up to Him in a Day whose length is fifty thousand years.

passages.title: 79:30 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: And after that He spread out the earth,

passages.title: 79:31 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: brought out of it its water and its pasture,

passages.title: 79:32 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: and set the mountains firmly in place,

passages.title: 7:54 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: Your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then rose above the Throne. He covers the day with the night, which follows it swiftly; and the sun, the moon and the stars are made to serve by His command. Creation and command are His alone. Blessed is Allah, Lord of all the worlds.

passages.title: 81:1 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: When the sun is wrapped up and its light is gone,

passages.title: 81:2 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: and when the stars fall and lose their light,

passages.title: 82:1 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: When the sky is split apart,

passages.title: 82:2 in plain words (an explanation, not a translation)
passages.text: and when the stars are scattered,
